newsitem.title: LAOS: FEATURE - Laos tries to defuse threat of war-era bombs.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Laos tries to defuse threat of war-era bombs.

text.p: In Laos, giant casings from American bombs are more than an ugly reminder of one of the heaviest aerial bombing campaigns in history.
They are part of everyday life.
Villagers fill split casings with soil and plant herbs and flowers in them. Others pile them vertically to build fences or support roof beams in their homes.
And here at the Nam Suang bomb-clearance training camp, they have found yet another use: a teaching tool.

In a giant sandbox, American military officers scatter casings and metal nails to teach Laotians how to detect and detonate bombs that landed more than 20 years ago but never exploded, posing a threat to children, farmers and fishermen.

Nearby, a young Lao medic wipes fake blood from an American soldier's chest and leg and plunges an intravenous needle into his arm, practising how to treat bomb-clearance experts injured in the line of work.
VIETNAM WAR'S DEADLY LEGACY
The camp, which is operated by the national bomb-clearing programme with assistance from the U.S. government, is a modern-day reminder of one of the darkest chapters in Lao history.

Between 1964 and 1973, Laos was the scene of protracted ground battles and heavy aerial bombardment as Americans tried to cut off North Vietnam's access to the Ho Chi Minh trail, which runs along eastern Laos.
During that period, the Americans launched more than 500,000 bombing missions, or the equivalent of one planeload of bombs every eight minutes around the clock for nine full years.
Many bombs never exploded, destroying lives years later when accidently detonated by a child or farmer.

The National Survey on the Socio-Economic Impact of Unexploded Ordnance (UXO) in Lao PDR, which is due to be released next week, has found bombs are scattered over 16 of 18 provinces and administrative districts and continue to cause 200 deaths and injuries annually.
About 11,000 Laotians have died or been injured by bombs since 1973, said Ian Mansfield, adviser to the National UXO Programme or Lao UXO, in an interview with Reuters.
About half of all incidents have been deadly, according to the year-long survey, which covered 8,000 of 11,000 Lao villages.
At the Nam Suang camp, that toll is fresh in the minds of the 78 students who receive medical, bomb clearance and community awareness training in the nine-week training course.
Anoulack Kittisack, 25, said the reports of so many injuries around the country prompted him to sign on for the nine-week training course.
Another student recalled throwing a baseball-sized bomblet with his friends as a child, thinking it was a toy, says Charles Kraus, coordinator of the U.S. Humanitarian Demining Office.
It exploded, shooting ball bearings into a group of the student's playmates, killing five of them.
FAMILIARITY BREEDS DANGEROUS SENSE OF SECURITY

The problem's pervasiveness has also led to a false sense of security on the part of many villagers, who are so accustomed to bombs they are no longer as frightened as they should be of their destructive power, said Mansfield.
"The problem in Laos is people have lived with the UXO problem for 25 years. It's always in the back of their minds...but it's something they've learned to live with," he said.
In the first four months of this year, Lao UXO, which is part of the Ministry of Labour, has destroyed 6,181 bombs and 11,384 other pieces of unexploded ordnance and removed 14 mines.
But it is slow work. Those efforts have resulted in the clearance of only 48.9 hectares (122 acres) in four provinces.
And Lao UXO, at only a year and a half old, is experiencing some growing pains -- it needs $2.8 million to meet a shortfall in its $9.8 million 1997 programme.
Still, more than 200 students have graduated from the Nam Suang camp, which has been open for a year, and more are in training.
Many are too young to remember the saturation bombing of the past but want to help fight its deadly modern-day consequences.
"The first reason I am here is to destroy UXO," Anoulack told Reuters. "The second is to save people from injury."
